title: Compare different orders of the same operations
chapter: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
goal: Compare two orders of the same operations using a general starting value.

scenes.visual: Run three through add two and double in both orders. Track the amount between each operation.
scenes.narration: Start with three. Add two and then double. Five becomes ten. Try the same start with the operations swapped. Double three first, then add two. Six becomes eight. The same steps can give different results when their order changes.

scenes.visual: Let several example inputs become a single tile labelled x, then lead the tile to two operation lanes.
scenes.narration: Testing more starting numbers might help us guess a pattern. A letter lets us explain the pattern for every starting number. We'll compare the two operation orders side by side and look for the part that changes.

scenes.visual: Build two unsolved lanes with add five and double. Hold the question and the input tile.
scenes.narration: Choose any starting number. Order A adds five and then doubles. Order B doubles and then adds five. Which order gives the bigger result, and by how much? Try one starting number before we compare them all.

scenes.visual: Attach a gold five to x, duplicate the entire bar, then collect its two gold tiles.
scenes.narration: Call the starting number x. In Order A, adding five makes a bar with an x part and a five part. Doubling makes two copies of that whole bar. Collect its parts. Two copies of x and two fives give two x plus ten.

scenes.visual: Double x alone and attach one five in a second lane. Pair the corresponding pieces with Order A.
scenes.narration: Order B doubles x first. That gives two copies of x. Add five once. Both orders now show two copies of the starting value and at least one five. Pair those matching pieces. The extra five in Order A is the entire difference.

scenes.visual: Replace the multiplier with negative two. Align the common terms, then measure the gap from negative ten to positive five.
scenes.narration: What if we multiply by negative two instead? In Order A, the five is multiplied too, so its contribution is negative ten. Order B still adds positive five. The common part is negative two x in both orders. Positive five is fifteen more than negative ten, so Order B now wins by fifteen.

scenes.visual: Rearrange two addition tiles, then two multiplication tiles, and show that their combined amount is unchanged.
scenes.narration: Two additions can swap because we still add the same total. Two multiplications can swap because their combined scale is the same. When you mix the two types of step, look closely at whether an amount added later gets scaled at all.

scenes.visual: Recall input, two orders, gap. Show the notebook operation lanes without either output.
scenes.narration: Give the start a letter. Write the two orders separately. Compare the parts that match and calculate the difference. In your notebook, compare subtracting four and then multiplying by three with multiplying by three and then subtracting four. Which gives the greater result, and by how much?

notebook_exercise: Compare subtracting 4 then multiplying by 3 with multiplying by 3 then subtracting 4. Which gives the greater result, and by how much?
notebook_answer: 3(x − 4) = 3x − 12 and 3x − 4. The second is always larger by 8.
